summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over ARCnet networks: the frame format, how link-local and automatically configured IPv6 addresses are formed, and the link-layer address option used in IPv6 neighbor discovery messages. It was later updated by RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: ARCnet is an old local network technology with very short addresses and only one multicast address. This document explains how IPv6 traffic is carried over it, and how a computer on an ARCnet network works out its own IPv6 address from the ARCnet address it was given.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets are carried on ARCnet, and how IPv6 addresses are built from ARCnet addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs a link-layer protocol to carry it, and ARCnet is a token-ring style network with an 8-bit address space and only one multicast address, so the way IPv6 packets are framed and the way IPv6 addresses are built both have to be spelled out for it.
tldr.mechanism: The document assigns the ARCnet system code C4 to IPv6, fixes a default maximum transmission unit of 9072 octets, and defines how an interface identifier is built from an ARCnet address so that link-local and autoconfigured addresses can be formed.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2497 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 8064, so the interface identifier rules here should be read together with that document.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content: This memo specifies a frame format for transmission of IPv6 packets and the method of forming IPv6 link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on ARCnet networks. It also specifies the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used by the Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages described in RFC 2461, when those messages are transmitted on an ARCnet.
sections.plainLanguage: The document covers three things: how an IPv6 packet is put into an ARCnet frame, how a computer builds its own IPv6 address from its ARCnet address, and how neighbour discovery messages carry that ARCnet address.

sections.title: The Frame Format
sections.content:
IPv6 packets are link layer fragmented and reassembled according to the ARCNET Packet Header Definition Standard, and a brief but sufficient discussion of this fragmentation method can be found in the earlier document on transmitting IP traffic over ARCNET networks.

The protocol ID, called the System Code in ARCnet terminology, assigned to IPv6 is C4 hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IPv6 packet goes into an ARCnet frame with a system code saying which protocol it carries, and the value for IPv6 is C4 in hexadecimal. Large packets are split and put back together at the link layer, following the ARCnet packet header standard.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
The maximum IPv6 packet length possible using this encapsulation method is 60480 octets. Since this length is impractical because of its worst case transmission time of several seconds, all ARCnet implementations on a given ARCnet network should agree on a smaller value. The default MTU for IPv6 packets on an ARCnet is 9072 octets.

In the presence of a router, this size MAY be changed by a Router Advertisement containing an MTU option. If a Router Advertisement is received with an MTU option specifying an MTU larger than 60480, or larger than a manually configured value less than 60480, that MTU option may be logged to system management but MUST be otherwise ignored.

If no router is available, the local MTU MUST be left at 9072 or MUST be manually configured to the same different value on all connected stations. Implementations MAY accept arriving IPv6 datagrams that are larger than their configured maximum transmission unit and are not required to discard them. If they cannot handle larger datagrams, they MAY log the event to system administration but MUST otherwise silently discard them.
sections.plainLanguage: The largest packet the method could carry is 60480 bytes, but sending one that size would take several seconds, so every implementation on the network is expected to agree on something smaller. The default is 9072 bytes, and a router can announce a different value.

sections.title: Building the Interface Identifier
sections.content:
If a node has an EUI-64 which is not used to form the Interface Identifier for any other interface, it SHOULD use that EUI-64 to form the Interface Identifier for its ARCnet interface. If that EUI-64 is in use for another interface attached to a different link, it MAY be used for the ARCnet interface as well. The Interface Identifier is then formed from the EUI-64 by complementing the Universal/Local bit, which is the next-to-lowest order bit of the first octet of the EUI-64.

When a node has no EUI-64 available for forming its ARCnet Interface Identifier, it MUST form that identifier as specified in the addressing architecture specification, in the section on links with a non-global identifier. That is, the 8-bit manually configured ARCnet address is appended to the 56 zero bits. For example, for an ARCnet interface with the configured address of 49 hexadecimal, the identifier is 56 zero bits followed by the eight bits 0001001, which results in the universal/local bit set to 0 to indicate local scope.

An IPv6 address prefix used for stateless auto-configuration of an ARCnet interface MUST have a length of 64 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IPv6 address ends with a part that is unique to the network card, called the interface identifier. On ARCnet there are two ways to make it: use the card's own hardware address if it has one, or simply pad the 8-bit ARCnet address with zeros. Either way the result is marked as local in scope.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses
sections.content: The IPv6 link-local address for an ARCnet interface is formed by appending the Interface Identifier, as defined above, to the prefix FE80::/64. The address therefore has ten bits of prefix, 54 bits of zeros and the 64-bit interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The address that only works on this one network is the usual FE80:: prefix followed by the interface identifier that was just described.

sections.title: Mapping IPv6 Addresses onto ARCnet
sections.content:
The procedure for mapping IPv6 addresses into ARCnet link-layer addresses is described in the neighbour discovery specification. The Source/Target link-layer address option has the form shown in the RFC when the link layer is ARCnet. The Type field is 1 for a Source Link-layer address and 2 for a Target Link-layer address. The Length field is 1, in units of 8 octets. The ARCnet address field holds the 8-bit ARCnet address in canonical bit order, followed by 5 octets of padding.

For multicast, ARCnet only provides one multicast address, 00 hexadecimal, so all IPv6 multicast addresses MUST be mapped to this address.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbour discovery messages carry the ARCnet address of the sender or receiver in a small option. Because ARCnet has only one multicast address, every IPv6 multicast group maps onto the same one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The method of derivation of Interface Identifiers from ARCnet addresses is intended to preserve local uniqueness when possible. However, there is no protection from duplication through accident or forgery.
sections.plainLanguage: Building the interface identifier from the ARCnet address keeps addresses different from each other in most cases, but nothing stops two of them being the same by accident or on purpose.

items.title: From a hardware address
items.text: Use the EUI-64 of the interface, with the universal/local bit complemented.

items.text: Append the 8-bit manually configured ARCnet address to 56 zero bits.
